title: Is the Bond Hedge Working? Bad Stock Days by Year
revision_note: FRED's SP500 and H.15 yields are not revised after publication.
methodology: A risk-off day is a day the S&P 500 fell at least 1%. For each calendar year, the table shows how many there were, the average S&P fall, and — for the yield tenor you pick — the average change in that yield in basis points and the share of those days it fell. A yield that falls is a bond price that rises: the share is the hedge working. 100% means bonds rallied on every bad stock day.

The fund column is the estimated price move of an intermediate Treasury fund on those days: −4.9 × the change in the 7-year yield, where 4.9 years is the average duration of Vanguard's VGIT (3- to 10-year Treasuries) and the 7-year yield stands in for the fund's own. It is an approximation, not the fund's actual return.

The correlation column is the year's correlation between the S&P's daily return and the daily change in the 10-year yield, over all sessions, not only bad days. Positive means stocks and yields fall together, so bond prices rise on bad stock days (the hedge works); negative means bond prices fall with stocks. Published stock–bond correlations usually use bond returns, which reverses the sign.
notes: The first calendar year in the data starts partway through, where FRED's ten-year window begins, and is labelled with its first date. The current year is labelled 'to date'.

The 2- and 5-year yields are offered because a real growth scare pulls rate-cut expectations forward, and those maturities are where the cuts are priced: the hedge can survive at the short end while failing at the long end.

Unpublished. FRED's SP500 is S&P Dow Jones Indices data, and S&P refused free permission to display index values on 2026-09-15 (catalog/sources/spglobal.json). This chart shows figures computed from those closes rather than the closes themselves, but the site's rule is that everything derived from S&P prices inherits the refusal, so it builds locally only (`scripts/dev.sh`).
FRED's SP500 covers only a rolling ten years, so no history before that exists here. The yields are FRED's H.15 constant-maturity series.
A day counts only if both the S&P and the Treasury yield report: the bond market is shut on some days stocks trade, so a return is measured between consecutive common dates.

presentation.summary: For each year: how often the S&P 500 fell 1% or more, and what Treasury yields did on those days.
